lines.trans: Excuse me, sir—would you like to come inside for a warm cup of tea?
Wait... our neighbour from the violin shop at number ten?!
You know each other, Mazen?!
Thirty years ago, he brought his violin here every Friday at six!
Wait—look at our old postcard: 'Save two chairs for the baker and the teacher'!
He was the music teacher who played Friday duets with your aunt!
He just asked me who finally finished the second half of her May waltz!
What did he say when he heard my sixteen bars through the window, Mazen?
He had tears in his eyes—he said it sounded just like her voice!
Did you invite him to our grand opening this Friday at six o'clock?!
He promised to bring his violin—and ten neighbours from down the street!
Ten extra neighbours?! Salma is going to need twice as many lemons by Friday!

meanings.note: Polite Arabic expression used both for 'excuse me' to get attention and 'you're welcome'.

examples.trans: We used the word عفواً.
This is another عفواً.

meanings.note: Polite Jordanian title for any man ('sir / Mr') as well as 'teacher' or 'professor'.

examples.trans: Please have a seat, sir.
Good morning, gentlemen.

meanings.note: Polite offer opener بتحب ('would you like to...?'), from حبّ (to love/like).

examples.trans: We used the word حبّ.
This is another حبّ.

تفضّل.gloss: to please come in / sit / go ahead / here you are

meanings.en: to please come in / sit / go ahead / here you are
meanings.note: Essential Jordanian hospitality verb used mostly in the imperative: تفضل (to a man), تفضلي (to a woman), تفضلوا (plural).

examples.trans: Please have a seat, ma'am!
Here you go, hot mint tea.

meanings.note: Used both before a noun ('inside the bag') and standalone ('inside').

examples.trans: Look inside the suitcase, Nour!
The water is flowing inside!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بشرب, بيشرب).

examples.trans: Drink hot tea first.

examples.text: شرب كل نقطة من شوربة الخضار.
examples.trans: He drank every drop of the vegetable soup.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: كاسات.

examples.trans: Please have a glass of hot mint tea.
He poured half a glass of orange juice.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: Please have a glass of hot mint tea.
There is black tea and coffee at breakfast.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: سخنة, plural: سخنين).

examples.trans: Drink a glass of hot tea first.
Pour the hot water into the pot.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بستنى, بيستنى).

examples.trans: Wait a moment, I have an idea!
The suitcase is still waiting for its owner.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: جيران.

examples.trans: All the neighbours on the street are kind.
Good morning, dear neighbour.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian possessive word ('belonging to'); agrees in gender: تبع (m.), تبعت (f.), تبعون (pl.).

examples.text: اليوم آخر يوم بأسبوع التجربة تبعك.
examples.trans: Today is the last day of your trial week.
My brother's piano teacher!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian noun for any retail shop or spot (pl. محلات).

examples.trans: Below is the signature of the antique shop.
There's a pastry shop next to the house.

كمان.gloss: also; too; again (كمان مرة once more)

meanings.en: also; too; again (كمان مرة once more)
meanings.note: Everyday Levantine word for 'also, too, more' (كمان مرة 'one more time / again').

examples.text: التفكير السريع أنقذ الفطور كمان مرة!
examples.trans: Quick thinking saved breakfast once again!
And I missed you too.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أرقام.

examples.trans: Here is your key, room number four.
Is there a phone number written on the paper?

meanings.note: Numeral 'ten'; short form عشر ('ashar) before a plural noun (عشر دقايق 'ten minutes').

examples.trans: You arrived ten minutes early.
Breakfast is from seven-thirty to ten.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بعرف, بيعرف).

examples.trans: I recognized your neat handwriting in two seconds!
Do you know anyone here in Amman?

meanings.note: After a plural verb, بعض means 'each other' (بننادي بعض 'we call each other').

examples.trans: We call each other by first name here.

examples.text: ما حكينا مع بعض من زمان.
examples.trans: We have not spoken with each other in a long time.

meanings.note: Placed directly before a name or title when addressing someone in Arabic (يا نور 'Nour!', يا أستاذ 'sir!') and in exclamations (يا سلام! 'wonderful!').

examples.trans: Good morning, Tariq!
Oh, how lovely the sun is after the rain!

meanings.note: Male given name of the guesthouse owner.

examples.trans: We used the word مازن.
This is another مازن.

meanings.note: Means 'before' (قبل الفطور) and with a time span 'ago' (قبل ساعة 'an hour ago', قبل شوي 'just now').

examples.text: علمت بيانو هون قبل خمسة وعشرين سنة.
examples.trans: I taught piano here twenty-five years ago.
Drink your coffee before the rush.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian numeral 'thirty'.

examples.trans: They have given us thirty days in the letter.
The bill is thirty-eight dinars.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: سنين.

examples.trans: The building is eighty years old.
I have not seen him for three years.

meanings.note: Arabic uses no 'is/are' in the simple present, while كان supplies the past ('was/were') and يكون / بيكون supplies future or modal 'be'.

examples.trans: How was the bus ride?

examples.text: تاني يوم ما رح يكون ممل!
examples.trans: The second day will not be boring!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بجيب, بيجيب).

examples.text: رح أجيب شراشف نظيفة من الخزانة.
examples.trans: I will bring clean sheets from the closet.

examples.text: أي علبة زبدة جبتي يا نور؟
examples.trans: Which tub of butter did you bring, Nour?

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian/Levantine word for 'here' (لهون 'to here', من هون 'from here').

examples.trans: Here we use this big ledger.
Stay right here a minute.

meanings.note: Before an indefinite singular noun كل means 'every' (كل يوم 'every day'); before a definite noun it means 'all / the whole' (كل الأسبوع 'all week').

examples.trans: Tell me everything I need to know.
Everyone is happy in the courtyard today.

meanings.note: Day of the week Friday, literally 'gathering day'.

examples.trans: We used the word جمعة.
This is another جمعة.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: ساعات.

examples.trans: What time is it right now, please?
We arrived an hour ago on the dot.

meanings.note: Numeral 'six'; short form ست (sitt) before a plural noun (ست سنين 'six years').

examples.trans: Room six is on the second floor.
I have six lemons in the basket.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'to see, look, check' (بشوف / شاف).

examples.trans: Look inside the suitcase, Nour!
I will see you tomorrow at breakfast.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: بطاقات.

examples.trans: There is a paper tag on the suitcase.
I wrote my name on the card.

meanings.note: Nisba adjective from بريد (mail); بطاقة بريدية means 'postcard'.

examples.trans: We used the word بريدي.
This is another بريدي.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: قديمة, plural: قدام).

examples.trans: The courtyard has an old jasmine tree.
The old hardware shop is past the bridge.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: The suitcase is safe and sound in the closet.
Preserving heritage is everyone's responsibility.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: كراسي.

examples.trans: We placed eight chairs around the tables.
I tightened the screw on the wooden chair.

meanings.note: Occupation pattern فعّال from خبز (bread), meaning 'baker'.

examples.trans: We used the word خبّاز.
This is another خبّاز.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian spelling/pronunciation of هذا ('this/that').

examples.trans: We used the word هادا.
This is another هادا.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun.

examples.trans: We found an old music book in the suitcase.
Gentle music is soothing in the evening.

meanings.note: Invariant spoken Jordanian relative pronoun ('who, which, that') for any gender or number.

examples.trans: That is what I want.
The inn that keeps a stranger's bag safe.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: Piano playing calms the nerves.
Whenever she finishes playing, she smiles.

meanings.note: From ثنائي (two-part/duo), used in music for duets.

examples.trans: We used the word ثنائي.
This is another ثنائي.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أيام.

examples.trans: Today the weather is sunny and warm in Amman.
Have a happy, successful day!

meanings.note: Everyday preposition 'with'; takes pronoun suffixes to express 'have on one's person' (معي 'I have with me', معك حق 'you are right').

examples.trans: You are right, Nour!
Goodbye! (lit. go with safety)

meanings.note: Arabic distinguishes father's sister (عمة, feminine of عمّ) from mother's sister (خالة).

examples.text: عمتي كانت تعزف عالبيانو كل يوم جمعة.
examples.trans: My paternal aunt used to play the piano every Friday.

examples.text: هاد الدفتر الأخضر هدية من عمتي.
examples.trans: This green notebook is a gift from my aunt.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بسأل, بيسأل).

examples.trans: Ask him what his name is on the phone!
I came down to ask about the sink water.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine word for 'now / right now' (pronounced halla' in Amman).

examples.trans: A taxi just stopped at the door now.
We will check the tag right now.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian question word for 'who?' (لمين 'whose? / for whom?').

examples.trans: Who left this envelope here?
Whose is this brown leather notebook?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بخلص, بيخلص).

examples.trans: I finished making the bed quickly!

examples.text: كل ما أخلص عزف كنا نحكي.
examples.trans: Whenever I finished playing, we used to chat.

meanings.note: Everyday adverb meaning 'finally / at last'.

examples.trans: We used the word أخيراً.
This is another أخيراً.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian form of نصف ('half'); used for half hours (السبعة ونص seven thirty) and quantities (نص كاسة half a glass).

examples.trans: Breakfast starts at seven thirty.

examples.text: بس نص كاسة عصير لو سمحت.
examples.trans: Just half a glass of juice, please.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: تانية, plural: تانيين).

examples.trans: Room four is on the second floor.
There is a second sheet behind the letter.

meanings.note: Everyday preposition meaning 'from', 'of', or 'than' after comparatives.

examples.trans: I am Salma from the kitchen.
Breakfast is from seven-thirty to ten.

meanings.note: Musical loanword (from French valse) for a triple-time piano or orchestral waltz.

examples.text: عزفت سعاد فالس هادي بغرفة القزاز.
examples.trans: Suad played a gentle waltz in the sunroom.

examples.text: عنوان الورقة القديمة هو فالس الساحة.
examples.trans: The title on the old sheet is Courtyard Waltz.

meanings.note: Jordan, Syria, Lebanon and Palestine use the old Syriac-derived month names: كانون التاني January ... أيار May ... أيلول September.

examples.trans: My birthday is in May.
In May the weather gets nice in Amman.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine question word for 'what?'.

examples.trans: What is that sound?
What is written on the sheet, Rami?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'to speak, talk, tell' (بحكي / حكى).

examples.trans: Salma chats with all the neighbours.
Tell me everything I need to know.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian conjunction 'when' (in statements, not questions).

examples.trans: Smile when the bell rings!
When I get nervous, my sentences turn long.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بسمع, بيسمع).

examples.trans: Did you hear the gate bell downstairs?
Inside the courtyard we hear the tree leaves.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian spoken number for 16 (adds -er before a counted noun: ستعشر سنة).

examples.trans: I did not rush bar sixteen at all!

examples.text: في ستعشر كرسي فاضي حول الشجرة.
examples.trans: There are sixteen empty chairs around the tree.

meanings.note: Standard Arabic conservatory/musicians' term (from Italian misura) for one bar of music.

examples.text: عزفت سعاد أول أربع مازورات من الفالس.
examples.trans: Suad played the first four bars of the waltz.

examples.text: اللحن بيوقف بنص المازورة الرابعة والعشرين.
examples.trans: The melody stops in the middle of the twenty-fourth bar.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: شبابيك.

examples.trans: The window overlooks the courtyard tree.
We painted the wooden shutters in summer.

meanings.note: Form II verb (بتدمّع / دمّعت) from دمع ('tears'). Used when someone's eyes well up with emotion.

examples.text: قبل ما تدمّع عيونك يا معلم، ساعدني!
examples.trans: Before your eyes get misty, boss, help me!
Her eyes watered with joy at the gift.

meanings.note: Feminine noun; also used in the delighted Jordanian exclamation يا عيني! ('oh my! / how lovely!').

examples.trans: Close your eyes and smell the coffee!
Oh my, look at that warm light in the courtyard!

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine conjunction introducing reported thoughts or clauses (MSA أن).

examples.trans: We used the word إنو.
This is another إنو.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: طالعة, plural: طالعين).

examples.trans: Count on me, I am heading right out!
We are going up to the third floor.

meanings.note: Spoken word for 'like': زيك 'like you'; زي ما 'just as, the way that'.

examples.trans: I want a glass of tea like yesterday.
Do it the way I taught you.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أصوات.

examples.trans: I heard the sound of rain on the window.
His voice is calm and polite on the phone.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بضبط, بيضبط).

examples.trans: Set the alarm for six, Tariq.
The plan worked out one hundred percent!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb عزم means 'to invite' someone to an event, meal, or coffee.

examples.trans: We used the word عزم.
This is another عزم.

meanings.note: Everyday preposition 'on, at, to'; before ال- it regularly contracts to عال- ('al- / 'a-).

examples.trans: Your glasses are on your forehead!
Say hello to Salma for me!

meanings.note: Official opening day or evening of a café, exhibition, or hall.

examples.text: افتتاح الكافيه رح يكون بآخر الأسبوع.
examples.trans: The café opening will take place at the end of the week.

examples.text: عزمنا كل الجيران على ليلة الافتتاح.
examples.trans: We invited all the neighbours to opening night.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: كبيرة, plural: كبار).

examples.trans: We use this big paper ledger.
You know older brothers well!

meanings.note: Active participle of إجا ('to come'): means 'on the way / arriving' (جايين 'they are coming') and after a time noun 'next' (الأسبوع الجاي 'next week').

examples.trans: The guests are coming down the stairs now.
We will see you next week!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: وعود.

examples.trans: We will come next week, promise!
He kept his promise and arrived on time.

meanings.note: Placed directly before an indefinite noun without ال- to mean 'the last' (آخر يوم 'the last day', آخر الساحة 'the far end of the courtyard').

examples.trans: The attic room is at the end of the floor.
Today is the last day of the week.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: شوارع.

examples.trans: Our guesthouse is on a quiet street in central Amman.
There are old stone streets in the quarter.

meanings.note: Placed directly after a noun in Jordanian to mean 'extra' (قطع زيادة extra pieces, الدرج الزيادة the extra stairs).

examples.trans: I brought two extra chairs for the courtyard.
I put a little extra mint in the tea.

meanings.note: Female given name belonging to the café's morning baker.

examples.trans: We used the word سلمى.
This is another سلمى.

meanings.note: Invariant spoken Levantine future marker placed before a subjunctive verb (without ب-).

examples.text: ضيفة غرفة أربعة رح تقعد كل الأسبوع.
examples.trans: Room four's guest will stay all week.

examples.text: تاني يوم ما رح يكون ممل!
examples.trans: The second day is not going to be boring!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بحتاج, بيحتاج).

examples.text: رني الجرس إذا احتجتي أي شي.
examples.trans: Ring the bell if you need anything.
An old house needs steady care.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أضعاف.

examples.trans: Today we baked double the usual amount.
The courtyard holds twice this number.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: كميات.

examples.trans: We need double the amount for tomorrow morning.
This quantity is enough for ten guests.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: ليمون.

examples.trans: The warm lemon cake is ready.
I squeezed half a lemon into the soup.

meanings.note: Core word in مع السلامة! ('goodbye!', literally 'with safety') and الحمد لله عالسلامة ('glad you arrived safely').

examples.trans: Goodbye, see you tomorrow!
Thank goodness for your safe arrival.
